data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Nauru uses the Australian dollar, so inflation is imported - and the early-2000s phosphate-economy distortions made it extreme: 19.3% in 2006 and a series high of 22.4% in 2009, followed by deflation of -3.4% in 2011 as the economy restructured. The 2010s were calmer (mostly 0-10%), but inflation picked up again to 9.3% in 2024 with a projected 6.1% for 2025. There is no domestic monetary policy; price stability depends on Australian conditions and on the government's ability to smooth costs using processing-centre and mining revenues.
debt_management: Nauru's debt history is the Pacific's most extreme: the IMF series (which starts in 2009; 2006-08 are missing) shows gross debt at 295.6% of GDP in 2009 and a series high of 298.9% in 2010 - the legacy of phosphate-era borrowing against a depleted resource. What followed was a two-decade workout: debt fell to 113% by 2015, 56.3% in 2020, and a projected 14.6% in 2025, driven by GDP growth ($0.03bn to $0.18bn), Australian processing-centre payments, and restructurings. The overhang is essentially cleared, but the episode is a cautionary tale about resource-curse borrowing. Note the 2006-08 data gap in the IMF series.

key_events.event: The IMF series carries no debt data for these years, reflecting the opacity of the phosphate-era debt overhang at its worst.
Australia reopened the offshore Regional Processing Centre, making asylum processing Nauru's main revenue source.
October: David Adeang became president, shifting the country's political direction.
January: severed ties with Taiwan and recognized Beijing, two days after Taiwan's presidential election.

outlook_next_decade: The debt workout is essentially complete, which is a genuine achievement, but Nauru's economy still rests on two fragile pillars: Australian processing-centre payments (subject to Canberra's politics) and phosphate remnants. Diversification options are minimal on a 21-square-kilometre island. The China switch may bring infrastructure finance. The base case is fiscal stability with high revenue volatility; the risk is a sudden loss of the processing-centre income that underwrites the budget.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
